title: Toward Interpretable Quantum Generators for Financial Returns through Problem-Informed Circuit Design
authors: Huijie Guan, Xuanhao Wang, Shengbin Wang, Jiale Zhang, Jian Ding, Shuxin Xie, Dongdong Li, Jianjian Gao, Hantao Sun, Wenhao Chu
abstract: When used as function approximators, quantum circuits often lack interpretability and face a fundamental trade-off between expressivity and trainability. We propose a problem-informed framework for financial return generation that uses relational structure and symmetry-inspired parameter sharing to guide the construction of quantum circuits with few trainable parameters and empirically testable operator roles. We evaluate three quantum generator architectures, referred to as ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, and structured time evolution, within a hybrid Wasserstein quantum generative adversarial network trained to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows. Across circuits with one to four layers and one to eight trainable coefficients, these generators recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features, while single-layer configurations remain competitive with deeper variants. Across matched depths, independently trained ZZ-CRX configurations exhibit a predominantly downward shift in median leverage relative to ZZ, consistent with the intended directional role of the controlled-rotation construction. The small number of coefficients also enables direct landscape analysis, revealing competing parameter preferences between marginal and temporal objectives and helping to explain the difficulty of finding parameter settings that perform well on both. These results provide an initial demonstration that structural assumptions can guide the design of compact quantum generators and link circuit architecture to observable statistical behaviour, motivating more systematic and parameter-efficient approaches to quantum circuit construction.
summary: This work proposes a novel, problem-informed framework to build interpretable quantum generators for financial time series data using a Quantum GAN. By incorporating structural assumptions like symmetry and directed couplings, the authors design compact quantum circuits that successfully model complex statistical features of Bitcoin returns. This demonstrates a path toward linking fundamental circuit architecture choices directly to observable, measurable statistical behavior.
main_problem: The paper addresses the interpretability and expressivity trade-off when using quantum circuits as function approximators for complex tasks like financial return generation.
main_result: The proposed problem-informed framework successfully guides the design of compact quantum generators that recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features of financial returns.
method: A hybrid Wasserstein Quantum Generative Adversarial Network (QGAN) is employed, utilizing problem-informed circuit design principles like symmetry-inspired parameter sharing.
model_or_system: The model uses quantum circuits (ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, structured time evolution) acting as expectation-value samplers within a QGAN framework to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows.
key_observables: Marginal and temporal distributional features, median leverage, and the structure of the parameter landscape.
important_parameters: Circuit depth (1 to 4 layers) and number of trainable coefficients (1 to 8).
main_assumptions: The design assumes that structural assumptions (e.g., nearest-neighbor couplings, directed controls) can guide the construction of compact, interpretable quantum generators.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the problem-informed generator design, mapping empirical financial structures (like ACF or leverage asymmetry) to specific quantum operators and predicting falsifiable outcomes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem-informed framework, details the QGAN setup and circuit architectures, evaluates performance against classical methods, and analyzes the resulting parameter landscapes to explain model behavior.
why_interesting: It demonstrates how imposing domain-specific physical or structural knowledge (problem-informed design) can constrain quantum circuit ansatzes, leading to more interpretable and parameter-efficient quantum models, which is a key goal in quantum machine learning.
